newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli PM says differences with Jordan natural.
newsitem.headline: Israeli PM says differences with Jordan natural.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday political differences with Jordan were natural and occurred "in the finest families".
He was reacting to a warning Jordan's King Hussein made in an interview with the Arabic daily Asharq al-Awsat that an absence of progress in peace talks could lead to war in the Middle East.
"I think it is inevitable that we will have differences here and there. It happens among friends and even in the finest families," Netanyahu told reporters in parliament.

"But I have no doubt in our commitment to peace with Jordan, to developing our political and economic relations and I am committed to a dialogue with King Hussein whom I see as a very important partner in peace with Israel," he said.

King Hussein, who made peace with Israel two years ago and is widely regarded as Israel's closest Arab ally, recalled the 1991 Gulf War when Iraq fired dozens of Scud missiles at the Jewish state and threatend to hit Israel with chemical weapons.

"In the current situation, if we do not stride strongly forward to achieve peace, everything imaginable can happen, including a revival of 1991 when Netanyahu wore his gas mask on television," he said in the interview published on Tuesday.
"The alternative to peace is more awful that we can ever imagine," the Jordanian monarch added.

On one occassion during the Gulf War, then deputy minister Netanyahu donned a gas mask while interviewed on CNN television as sirens heralded an Iraqi missile attack. The scuds Iraq fired during the war all had conventional warheads.

"The main question now is what are we going to do? Does Israel want to return to the fortress mentality and an arrogant feeling of power? I've had the chance to know the Israelis quite well and I'm worried about them," the king said.

Hussein joined Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Washington for an emergency peace summit organised last week by the United States after an eruption of violence between Israeli troops and Palestinians left 73 people dead.
Arabs accuse Netatnyahu, who ousted Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shimon Peres in elections last May, of dragging his feet in peace talks and refusing to implement agreements with the Palestinians.

"I just hope that he (Netanyahu) realises that he has to deal with Arafat and the Palestinians as equal partners and not one who is of a lower level that he has to look down upon," Hussein said in the interview.
